1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: Basic information: Male patient, 50 years old, farmer, was admitted to our hospital on Day 0, with the chief complaint of “cough, sputum production, and hemoptysis for 4 months, worsening for 2 weeks.” History of present illness: 4 months before admission, the patient developed paroxysmal cough, sputum production, and hemoptysis without an obvious trigger, approximately 3-4 times/day, consisting of blood-streaked sputum, bright red in color, small in amount, and easily expectorated. The cough had no obvious day-night or seasonal pattern. He did not pay attention to it and did not seek diagnosis or treatment. Two weeks before admission, the patient’s paroxysmal cough, sputum production, and hemoptysis worsened, approximately 10-12 times/day, with about 7-8 ml of hemoptysis each time, dark red in color, accompanied by blood clot formation, and easily expectorated, accompanied by exertional shortness of breath; he became short of breath after climbing three flights of stairs, accompanied by nausea, and presented to a county hospital. Blood routine + CRP showed: WBC 13.5×10^9/L, NE 82.5%, CRP 30.69mg/L. Chest CT suggested possible inflammatory infection of the right lung, and he was referred to a municipal hospital. Blood routine + CRP showed: WBC 10.84×10^9/L, NE 76.6%, CRP 22.3mg/L; PCT: 0.081ng/ml, ESR: 23mm/h. Non-contrast and contrast-enhanced chest CT: lesion in the anterior segment of the right upper lobe, considered likely inflammation with possible localized abscess and atelectasis. He was diagnosed with “pulmonary infection.” From Day -15 to Day -8, cefotaxime was given for anti-infective treatment, supplemented with expectorant treatment and other management; the symptoms of cough, sputum production, and hemoptysis improved slightly. He was then referred again to a hepatobiliary hospital. Blood routine + CRP showed: WBC 10.85×10^9/L, NE 57.9%, CRP 11.53mg/L. Non-contrast and contrast-enhanced lung CT: 1. Inflammation in the right upper lobe with indistinct margins and abscess formation in the anterior segment. He was diagnosed with “lung abscess.” From Day -7 to Day -1, ceftriaxone and piperacillin-tazobactam were given for anti-infective treatment. The symptoms of cough, sputum production, and hemoptysis did not improve significantly. Repeat blood routine + CRP on Day -2 showed: WBC 12.11×10^9/L, NE 66.7%, CRP 7.9mg/L. For further treatment, he presented to our hospital, and the outpatient department planned to admit him with the diagnosis of “hemoptysis, cause to be determined.” The patient had lost about 2 kg over the past half month. Past history showed: self-administered dexamethasone 5mg BIW for 30 years because of osteoarthralgia; no further steroids were taken after admission, with occasional complaints of joint pain; “hypertension” for 4 years, usually taking “amlodipine 5mg qd” regularly by mouth; “type 2 diabetes mellitus” for 4 years, with highest random blood glucose 25mmol/l, regularly taking “gliclazide 60mg QD, metformin 0.5g QD” by mouth, with monitored preprandial blood glucose fluctuating around 10mmol/l; “status post bilateral cataract surgery” for 3 years. Old fractures of parts of the bilateral ribs were found half a month ago (specific trauma history unknown). In addition, during hospitalization at a municipal hospital 2 weeks earlier, markedly elevated AFP was found; further PET-CT suggested possible primary liver cancer in the right liver. One week earlier, hepatitis B serology at a hepatobiliary hospital suggested “hepatitis B small three positive,” with HBV DNA negative; he is currently taking entecavir 0.5mg QD orally for anti-HBV treatment. The patient reported no remarkable personal or family history. Physical examination on admission: T: 36.5℃; P: 109 beats/min; R: 21 breaths/min; BP: 94/68mmHg; SPO2: 93% (FiO2:21%). Normal development, well nourished, cushingoid facies, clear consciousness, cooperative on examination. Superficial veins throughout the body were slightly engorged. No enlargement of superficial lymph nodes throughout the body. No scleral icterus bilaterally, corneas clear, bilateral pupils equal, round, approximately 3mm in diameter, with brisk light reflexes. Coarse breath sounds in both lungs; no dry or wet rales were heard in either lung. Heart rate 109 beats/min, regular rhythm, no pathologic murmurs heard in any valve auscultation area. Abdomen flat and soft, without tenderness or rebound tenderness. Liver and spleen were not palpable below the costal margin, Murphy’s sign negative, no percussion tenderness over the liver or kidney regions. Bowel sounds 4 times/min. Limbs moved freely; bilateral proximal metacarpophalangeal joints were slightly swollen and tender; muscles slightly atrophied; no digital clubbing; no edema in either lower extremity. Ancillary examinations: (Day -20, county hospital) Chest CT: possible inflammatory infection of the right lung. (Day -14, municipal hospital) Tumor markers: CEA 7.15ng/ml, CA199 70.99u/ml, AFP 15987ng/ml, IGE 1459ng/ml. (Day -14, municipal hospital) Non-contrast and contrast-enhanced chest CT: 1. Lesion in the anterior segment of the right upper lobe, with indistinct margins, considered likely inflammation with possible localized abscess and atelectasis; coexistence of other lesions cannot be excluded. 2. Small linear opacity in the lingular segment of the left upper lobe; 3. Mass shadow in the anterior right hepatic lobe included in the scan, with poorly defined margins, considered possibly tumor; 4. Multiple small hepatic cysts. (Day -14, municipal hospital) PET-CT: 1. Mass-like mixed-density shadow in the right hepatic lobe, with mildly increased metabolism, primary liver cancer is considered first; other possibilities remain to be excluded; 2. Linear shadow in the left upper lobe; patchy shadow in the anterior segment of the right upper lobe with cystic low-density shadow, with mildly increased metabolism, considered possibly infection with localized abscess. (Day -10, municipal hospital) Echocardiography: slightly enlarged left atrium, thickened posterior wall of the left ventricle, EF 69.9%. (Day -6, hepatobiliary hospital) Hepatitis B serology: quantitative hepatitis B surface antigen 1049.51IU/ml, quantitative hepatitis B e antibody 0.34PEIU/ml, quantitative hepatitis B core antibody >25IU/ml, quantitative HBV DNA negative. (Day -6, hepatobiliary hospital) Tumor markers: CEA 7.5ng/ml, CA199 56.1u/ml, AFP >2000ng/ml, abnormal prothrombin 503mAU/ml. (Day -6, hepatobiliary hospital) Non-contrast and contrast-enhanced lung CT: 1. Inflammation in the right upper lobe, with indistinct margins, abscess formation in the anterior segment; 2. Old fractures of parts of the bilateral ribs; 3. Space-occupying lesion in hepatic segment V. (Day -6, hepatobiliary hospital) Non-contrast and contrast-enhanced upper abdominal MRI: 1. Multiple space-occupying lesions in hepatic segments VIII-IV, considered hepatocellular carcinoma, suspicious tumor thrombus in the right anterior branch of the portal vein, and the lesions are closely related to the gallbladder; 2. Persistently enhancing small nodular shadow in hepatic segment VII, hemangioma? 3. Heterogeneous fatty liver, multiple small hepatic cysts; 4. Bilateral renal cysts; 5. Nodular shadow within the L2 vertebral body.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: On Day +13, the BALF mNGS result reported detection of Mycobacterium gordonae.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has had cough, sputum production, and hemoptysis for 4 months, with marked worsening over the past 2 weeks. Imaging has repeatedly shown right upper lobe consolidation with abscess-/necrosis-like changes. Multiple courses of conventional antibacterial therapy resulted in only slight improvement or no obvious improvement, and on Day +12 the patient again developed recurrent fever with a maximum temperature of 39.3℃, suggesting a persistent and active infection. The patient also has an immunocompromised background, including 30 years of long-term oral dexamethasone use and poorly controlled diabetes. Routine sputum culture and early BALF culture both failed to detect pathogenic organisms, and TB-SPOT was negative but could not explain the entire clinical picture. Therefore, BALF mNGS is needed to broaden the scope of etiologic screening and to look for bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi, or pathogens of mixed infection that are not easily detected by routine culture. Selection of a BALF specimen can directly reflect pathogens in the local pulmonary lesion and is particularly suitable for a focal right upper lobe lesion, with no neoplasm seen on bronchoscopy but the most prominent blood staining at the right upper lobe bronchial orifice. The clinical purpose of this test is to clarify the etiologic direction as soon as possible, distinguish among common bacterial infection, TB/nontuberculous mycobacterial infection, and opportunistic infection, provide a basis for whether subsequent treatment should be changed to anti-nontuberculous mycobacterial therapy and whether to continue broad-spectrum antibacterial agents alone, and reduce the risk of blind invasive procedures and empiric medication in the setting of persistent hemoptysis, comorbid liver cancer, and poor overall condition.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: On Day +14, the sputum culture result from our hospital detected nontuberculous mycobacteria.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient's main manifestations were chronic cough, sputum production, and recurrent hemoptysis, with a disease course of up to 4 months. The imaging lesion was located in the right upper lobe and had shown no absorption over a prolonged period. Multiple previous anti-infective treatments with beta-lactams had limited efficacy, suggesting that chronic pathogens such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis or nontuberculous mycobacteria should be strongly considered. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, and sputum specimens were easy to obtain and could be collected repeatedly, making them suitable as a basic test for etiologic screening of respiratory mycobacterial infection. On prior bronchoscopy, no mass was seen. Routine BALF/sputum culture had at one point failed to detect common pathogenic bacteria, whereas BALF mNGS had already suggested mycobacterial clues. At this time, continuing sputum culture would help provide etiologic confirmation using another type of clinical specimen and determine whether there was persistent airway shedding of organisms, rather than incidental detection in a single lavage specimen. After sputum culture detected nontuberculous mycobacteria, it could further differentiate a persistent lung abscess-like lesion, lung cancer, pulmonary TB, and common bacterial infection, which is crucial for establishing the diagnosis of pulmonary nontuberculous mycobacterial disease and also provides a basis for deciding whether subspecialty referral, further drug susceptibility testing, and formulation of a long-term combination antimycobacterial treatment regimen are needed.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: On Day +15, the sputum culture + antimicrobial susceptibility test report from a pulmonary specialty hospital showed: the nontuberculous mycobacteria susceptibility results indicated susceptibility to clarithromycin, linezolid, and amikacin; intermediate susceptibility to moxifloxacin; and resistance to streptomycin, ethambutol, ciprofloxacin, rifabutin, doxycycline, rifampin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, isoniazid, and ethionamide.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: After BALF mNGS suggested mycobacteria and sputum culture at our hospital had already detected nontuberculous mycobacteria, the clinical question further shifted from "whether a special pathogen is present" to "whether this pathogen is the causative organism and how to use targeted antimicrobial therapy precisely." In this patient, the disease course was prolonged, hemoptysis was significant, and there had been recurrent fever; imaging showed a right upper lobe abscess-/necrosis-like lesion, and the response to multiple empiric anti-infective treatments was poor, indicating that if the regimen is not adjusted according to drug susceptibility results, continued empiric treatment will likely be ineffective. Different species and different strains of nontuberculous mycobacteria have markedly different resistance profiles, and detection of the pathogen alone cannot guide a specific regimen; in particular, because the patient also has diabetes mellitus, long-term steroid exposure, and a background of liver cancer and hepatitis B, subsequent treatment must balance efficacy, adverse effects, and medication-related risks, so sputum culture combined with antimicrobial susceptibility testing is ضروری. The core role of this testing is to determine susceptibility and resistance to macrolides, amikacin, linezolid, fluoroquinolones, and other drugs, help rule out continued use of ineffective agents, support development of an individualized combination treatment regimen, and provide a key basis for explaining prior anti-infective treatment failure, predicting efficacy, and assessing tolerability and risk during subsequent long-term treatment.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: On Day +12, recurrent fever developed, with a maximum temperature of 39.3°C. On Day +13, BALF mNGS results were reported as detecting Mycobacterium gordonae. On Day +14, sputum culture at our hospital was reported as detecting nontuberculous mycobacteria. On Day +15, sputum culture and drug susceptibility testing from a pulmonary hospital were reported as follows: the nontuberculous mycobacterial susceptibility results indicated susceptibility to clarithromycin, linezolid, and amikacin; intermediate susceptibility to moxifloxacin; and nonsusceptibility to streptomycin, ethambutol, ciprofloxacin, rifabutin, doxycycline, rifampin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, isoniazid, and ethionamide.

diagnostic_basis: Past history of diabetes mellitus with poor glycemic control, and a long-term history of glucocorticoid use. Physical examination showed Cushingoid facies. Laboratory testing showed markedly elevated AFP. PET-CT: 1. A mass-like mixed-density lesion was seen in the right hepatic lobe, with mildly increased metabolic activity; primary hepatocellular carcinoma is the first consideration. In combination with his medical history, immunosuppression was considered, placing him in a high-risk population for infection. Empiric treatment with multiple antibiotics resulted in no obvious improvement in symptoms.
Chest CT showed a right lung abscess, with large-caliber vessels coursing through the surrounding area; hemoptysis was considered possibly due to the presence of large vessels at the lesion site.

During hospitalization, sputum mycobacterial culture indicated nontuberculous mycobacteria; nontuberculous mycobacteria were detected in both sputum cultures, in conjunction with clinical symptoms, signs, and related examinations
Conventional anti-infective therapy was ineffective, and body temperature returned to normal after anti-NTM treatment.

treatment_plan: Changed to azithromycin 0.5 g po qd + rifampin 0.6 g po qd + ethambutol 0.9 g po qd + amikacin sulfate 600 mg ivgtt QD regimen for standardized treatment of nontuberculous mycobacterial disease
Refer to interventional radiology for initial hepatic arterial chemoembolization + bronchial artery embolization for hemostasis, followed by surgical treatment after the NTM infection is controlled
treatment_response: After treatment, the patient's body temperature gradually decreased to normal.
Repeat chest CT on Day +17 showed no obvious reduction in the lesions, suggesting a suboptimal treatment response.
Post-discharge follow-up: after oral antibiotics, the patient developed adverse reactions such as decreased appetite and had poor tolerance to long-term antibiotic therapy.
